subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the birth rate measure?
options: The number of live births per 1000 people per year
The total number of children a woman has
The number of live births per 100 women per year
The percentage of the population under 15
questions.explain: Birth rate is expressed as the number of live births per 1000 of the population in a year.

questions.q: How is the rate of natural increase of a population calculated?
questions.explain: Natural increase is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate, excluding migration.

questions.q: Which stage of the Demographic Transition Model has both a high birth rate and a high death rate, giving a stable low population?
questions.explain: In Stage 1 high birth and high death rates roughly balance, keeping total population low and fluctuating.

questions.q: What is population density?
options: The average number of people per unit area, e.g. per km²
The total number of people in a country
The way people are spread across an area
The number of births each year
questions.explain: Density is the total population divided by the total area, usually given as people per square kilometre.

questions.q: In calculating the dependency ratio, which age groups are counted as the dependent population?
questions.explain: The young (under 15) and the elderly (65+) are the non-working dependants supported by the working-age population.

questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 32 per 1000 and a death rate of 12 per 1000. What is its rate of natural increase?
questions.explain: Natural increase = 32 − 12 = 20 per 1000, which equals 2.0%.

questions.q: What is a 'push' factor in migration?
options: A negative condition that forces or encourages people to leave an area
An attractive feature that draws people to a new area
A government payment to encourage migration
questions.explain: Push factors, such as unemployment or war, are the disadvantages that make people want to move away from an area.

questions.q: Which of the following is best described as a pull factor for rural to urban migration?
options: More job opportunities in the city
Drought and crop failure in the countryside
Lack of services in the village
questions.explain: Pull factors attract migrants; greater employment in cities draws people from rural areas.

questions.q: Which term describes a person forced to flee across an international border to escape war or persecution?
questions.explain: A refugee is a forced migrant who leaves their country because of danger such as war or persecution.

questions.q: A skilled worker chooses to move from Poland to the UK for higher wages. How is this migrant best classified?
questions.explain: Moving by choice mainly for better pay makes this a voluntary, economic (and international) migration.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly ranks settlements from smallest to largest in the settlement hierarchy?
questions.explain: The hierarchy rises from isolated dwelling and hamlet, through village and town, up to city and conurbation.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'threshold population' of a service?
options: The minimum number of people needed for the service to run profitably
The maximum distance people will travel to the service
The total population of the settlement
The number of workers a service employs
questions.explain: Threshold population is the minimum number of customers required to make a service viable.

questions.q: A settlement has a hospital, a university and a department store. What does this indicate about the settlement?
options: It is high in the hierarchy with a large sphere of influence
It is a low-order settlement such as a hamlet
It has a very small threshold population
questions.explain: High-order services like hospitals and universities need large thresholds and serve a wide area, indicating a high-order settlement.

questions.q: What does the 'sphere of influence' (market area) of a settlement mean?
options: The area served by a settlement and its services
The land on which the settlement is built
The number of shops in the settlement
questions.explain: The sphere of influence is the surrounding area whose people use the settlement's services.

questions.q: What is found in the Central Business District (CBD) of a typical city?
options: Shops, offices and high land values
questions.explain: The CBD is the commercial core with shops and offices and the highest land values due to its accessibility.

questions.q: In Burgess's concentric zone model, how does land use change moving outward from the CBD?
options: Older inner-city housing gives way to newer, lower-density suburbs
Housing gets progressively older and more crowded
The CBD is repeated at each ring
Industry surrounds the outermost residential zone
questions.explain: Burgess's model shows the CBD at the centre, with housing generally becoming newer and less dense towards the suburbs.

questions.q: A planner notes traffic congestion, air pollution and a shortage of housing in a large city. These are best described as:
questions.explain: Congestion, pollution and housing shortages are common problems generated by rapid urban growth.

questions.q: What is urbanisation?
options: The increase in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities
The movement of people out of cities to the countryside
The growth of farming in rural areas
The spread of cities into surrounding farmland
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the rising share of a country's population living in urban rather than rural areas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a major cause of rapid urbanisation in many lower-income countries?
options: Rural to urban migration in search of work
People retiring to quiet rural villages
questions.explain: Large-scale movement of rural people to cities seeking jobs and services drives rapid urbanisation.

questions.q: Rapid urban growth in low-income countries often leads to the development of squatter settlements (shanty towns). Why?
options: Migrants arrive faster than adequate housing and services can be provided
Cities deliberately plan low-density luxury housing
The urban birth rate falls sharply
Wealthy residents move into self-built homes
questions.explain: When in-migration outpaces formal housing supply, newcomers build informal squatter settlements on the city edge or unused land.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Geography (0460) syllabus; Population & Settlement
